blocks.text: Some MCP sessions end in seconds. Others run for hours, sometimes days, carrying an agent through a task that unfolds slowly.
A session like that runs into problems a short one never has to think about, most of all a context window that keeps quietly filling up.

This lesson looks at what makes a session long running, why the context window becomes a real constraint over time, and how compression, checkpointing, and a clear sense of when to stop all work together to keep it healthy.
1. What Makes a Session Long Running

blocks.alt: A long running session accumulates many turns over extended time

blocks.text: A session earns the label long running when it is measured in hours or days rather than minutes, and when the work inside it spans many separate turns instead of one quick exchange.
Duration alone is not the whole story. What matters more is that meaningful state, decisions made, files touched, steps completed, has built up inside the session and needs to survive.

items: An agent working through a large codebase migration across an entire afternoon
A research assistant gathering and cross checking sources over several hours
A monitoring agent that stays connected and reacting for days at a time
A support session that gets picked up, paused, and returned to over a shift

blocks.text: 2. Where the Time Actually Goes
Long running sessions rarely stay busy every second. Much of the elapsed time is waiting, for a tool to finish, for a human to respond, for a scheduled check to come due.
That waiting is exactly why keep-alive, covered in the Transport lesson, matters so much here, a connection can sit idle for long stretches and still needs to be proven alive.

blocks.text: 3. The Growing Context Window Problem

blocks.alt: The context window keeps growing as a long session continues

blocks.text: Every turn a long running session takes adds more text to the conversation, the model request, the tool calls it makes, the results those calls return.
None of that text goes away on its own. Left unmanaged, a session that runs long enough will eventually try to fit more into the context window than the window can hold.
This is the central tension of a long session. The work that makes it valuable is the same work that fills up the space it needs to keep going.
4. Every Turn Adds Weight
Not every turn adds the same amount. A short confirmation costs almost nothing, while a tool call that returns a large file or a long log dump can cost thousands of tokens in one step.
Over a long session these costs add up, so the growth curve is rarely smooth, it tends to have a steady slow climb interrupted by sudden jumps.

blocks.title: Growth is lumpy, not linear
blocks.content: Plan for the occasional large tool result or file read, not just the average turn, since a handful of big turns can do more damage than hundreds of small ones.

blocks.text: 5. Keep-Alive Solves a Different Problem
Keep-alive answers one narrow question, is the connection still there. It says nothing about whether the conversation riding on top of that connection is still a healthy size.
A session can have a perfectly healthy, actively confirmed connection and still be carrying a context window that is dangerously close to full.

items: Keep-alive confirms the pipe is open
Keep-alive says nothing about how much is flowing through that pipe
A silent but healthy connection can still be attached to an unhealthy amount of accumulated context

blocks.text: 6. Pairing Keep-Alive With Compression

blocks.alt: Keep-alive keeps the connection open while compression keeps the context small

blocks.text: A long running session needs both disciplines running side by side, one watching the connection, the other watching the content.
Keep-alive keeps the session reachable. Compression, through summarization, keeps what is reachable actually usable once the model has to read it.

Neither one substitutes for the other. A session with only keep-alive can stay connected while silently becoming too bloated to reason over well, and a session with only compression can shrink its content perfectly while nobody notices the connection died an hour ago.

code.content:
async def long_session_loop(session):
    while session.active:
        await ping_if_due(session)               # keep-alive, from the Transport lesson
        await compress_if_over_budget(session)    # context compression
        await checkpoint_if_due(session)
        await handle_next_turn(session)

blocks.text: 7. Rolling Summarization

blocks.alt: Old turns are rolled up into a running summary as new turns arrive

blocks.text: The most common way to keep a long session context from overflowing is rolling summarization, folding older turns into a compact summary as new ones arrive.
Instead of keeping every raw turn forever, the session keeps a short running summary plus only the most recent turns in full detail.

code.content:
def roll_summary(history, keep_recent=6):
    if len(history) <= keep_recent:
        return history
    older = history[:-keep_recent]
    recent = history[-keep_recent:]
    summary = summarize(older)
    return [{"role": "system", "content": summary}] + recent

blocks.text: 8. What to Keep in Full and What to Fold Away
Not everything should be compressed at the same rate. Decisions, commitments, and open questions tend to matter for the whole session and deserve to survive summarization intact.
Routine back and forth, clarifying questions that already got answered, tool calls that succeeded without incident, can usually be folded down hard without losing anything anyone will need later.

items: Keep in full: firm decisions, agreed constraints, unresolved questions
Fold down: successful routine tool calls, resolved clarifications, restated context
Fold down hardest: large raw tool outputs once their relevant conclusion has been extracted

blocks.text: 9. Checkpointing Progress

blocks.alt: A checkpoint captures session progress at a point in time

blocks.text: Compression protects the context window. Checkpointing protects the work itself, so a long task does not have to start over if something interrupts it.
A checkpoint is a saved snapshot of where a task actually stands, written somewhere durable outside the conversation itself.

blocks.title: Checkpoints are not full transcripts
blocks.content: A checkpoint should capture enough to resume correctly, not every word exchanged along the way, that is what summarization is for.

blocks.text: 10. What Belongs in a Checkpoint
A useful checkpoint answers one question clearly, if the session vanished right now, what would a fresh process need to pick this up correctly.
That usually means progress markers rather than conversation, since raw dialogue is exactly what summarization already compresses separately.

items: Which steps are done and which remain
Any decisions or parameters that must not be re asked
Enough identifying detail to reconnect to external state, a file path, a ticket id, a database key
A timestamp, so staleness can be judged later

blocks.text: 11. Resuming Cleanly After an Interruption

blocks.alt: A session resumes cleanly from its last checkpoint after an interruption

blocks.text: Resuming a long task is only as good as the checkpoint it resumes from. A vague or stale checkpoint turns a resume into a guessing game.
The safest resume pattern loads the last checkpoint, confirms it still looks valid, and then continues from the recorded step rather than the very beginning.
This pattern only works well if each step is safe to treat as already done or not started, so idempotent steps make checkpointing far easier to trust.
12. How Often to Checkpoint
Checkpointing too rarely defeats the purpose, an interruption right before the next checkpoint still costs a large amount of redone work.
Checkpointing too often adds overhead and can slow down the very task it is meant to protect, especially if each checkpoint write is slow or expensive.

blocks.text: 13. Signs a Session Is Wearing Thin
Some sessions announce their own decline. Responses get slower, summaries start losing detail that used to be there, and the model begins re asking things it already answered.
These are not random glitches, they are usually symptoms of a context window that has been compressed past a useful point or a session carrying far more history than it needs.

items: Noticeably slower responses as the assembled context grows
The model forgetting or contradicting an earlier decision
Summaries that keep getting vaguer with every compression pass
Repeated re confirmation of things already settled

blocks.text: 14. When to End a Session and Start Fresh

blocks.alt: A session wearing thin points toward ending it and starting fresh

blocks.text: Not every long session should be kept alive indefinitely. Sometimes the healthier choice is to close it out and start a new one with a clean, deliberately built context.
A natural point to end a session is once the original task is genuinely finished, or once compression has been leaned on so many times that confidence in the summary is fading.

blocks.title: Starting fresh is not failure
blocks.content: A new session that starts from a clear checkpoint and a short, deliberate summary is often healthier than one old session stretched far past what compression can gracefully handle.

blocks.text: 15. Designing a Long Session From Day One
The sessions that age well are the ones built with all of this in mind from the start, not patched together after the context window first overflows.
That means keep-alive running from the first idle moment, summarization triggered on a clear budget rather than an emergency, and checkpoints written on a schedule the task can actually afford.

items: Decide the checkpoint frequency before the task starts, not after the first failure
Set a compression trigger tied to a token budget, not a vague sense that things feel long
Write down, in advance, what would justify ending the session early

blocks.text: Worked Example
Picture an agent asked to migrate a large codebase to a new logging library, a task expected to take most of a day.
By hour three, the session has touched forty files, and the raw turn history alone would already be pressing against the context budget.

A laptop restart interrupts the session right after that checkpoint is written. The next run loads this file, sees three services are done, and resumes at the fourth instead of starting the migration over.
Because the conversation history was already being rolled into a running summary, the resumed session does not need the full transcript either, just the summary and this small checkpoint.
Common Mistakes

items: Treating keep-alive as if it also protects the content of the conversation
Compressing so aggressively that decisions and constraints get lost along with the noise
Checkpointing only the conversation text instead of the actual task progress
Waiting for a failure to happen before deciding how often to checkpoint
Keeping one session running indefinitely long after the original task ended

blocks.text: Practice
Take a task you expect to run for several hours and sketch, on paper, when it would checkpoint, when it would compress, and what would make you end the session early.

items: Pick a checkpoint interval and justify it against how expensive a redo would be
Decide what must survive summarization in full and what can be folded away
Write the one condition that would make you close the session instead of extending it

blocks.text: Key Takeaway

A long running session stays healthy when three habits work together, a keep-alive check that confirms the connection is still there, compression that keeps the growing context usable, and checkpoints that let real progress survive an interruption.
